intro: Chicago is a young city on old prairie, and its oldest trees are the prairie's survivors: bur oaks that stood here before the city had a name. One shaded the Midway while the 1893 World's Fair rose around it, and a Norwood Park savanna remnant may be older than the United States. Out in the county's forest preserves stand ranked champions, among them hackberries and white oaks. The famous zoo oak fell in 2023. Eleven of the thirteen are free; the two golf-course champions generally need a green fee.
meta_description: Chicago's remarkable trees: prairie bur oaks older than the city, and Cook County's forest preserve champions, from hackberries to white oaks.
question_meta: Chicago's oldest trees are the bur oaks of Union Ridge Cemetery, estimated at 325 to 375 years. Their story, and 12 more remarkable trees.
question_answer: Chicago's oldest known trees are the bur oaks of the Union Ridge Cemetery savanna in Norwood Park, estimated by one expert survey at 325 to 375 years, older than the United States. The most storied is the bur oak on the Midway Plaisance in Hyde Park, which stood before the 1893 World's Fair was laid out around it.
question_context: Chicago's relationship with old trees is mostly a story of what the prairie kept. The city itself is young, incorporated in 1837, and it burned in 1871, so almost nothing planted stands out for age. What survives is what was already here: bur oaks, the prairie's fire-resistant veterans, in the few corners the city never quite got around to flattening. The best known of them, the bur oak at Lincoln Park Zoo that generations called Chicago's oldest tree, was cut down in May 2023 after it died, which quietly promoted the others. The Midway oak in Hyde Park carries a genuine dispute, one university account says it was planted for the 1893 fair, others say the fair was built around it, and its page gives both versions. The Union Ridge savanna's ages rest on a single expert's estimate and say so. That honesty matters here more than in most cities, because the register Illinois keeps for its champion trees records size, not age, and so does the county's own; a champion is not automatically ancient.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Chicago?
faq.a: The bur oaks of the Union Ridge Cemetery savanna in Norwood Park, estimated at 325 to 375 years by the one expert survey that dated them. The estimate is diameter-based rather than core-based, and the page says so.

faq.q: What happened to the famous oak at Lincoln Park Zoo?
faq.a: The bur oak that was long called Chicago's oldest tree died and was cut down in May 2023. It is not on this list; the trees that are, are the ones you can still stand under.

faq.q: Are Chicago's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: Eleven of the thirteen are free. The Midway oak and the Wooded Island grove stand in public parks, Union Ridge is a cemetery open in daylight hours, and the forest preserve champions stand on public preserve land. The champion boxelder and the champion red pine stand on public golf courses, where a green fee is generally needed to walk the course; ask at the clubhouse.

faq.q: Why are they almost all bur oaks?
faq.a: Because the bur oak is the prairie's survivor: thick corky bark made it the one tree that shrugged off the prairie fires that cleared everything else. What was here before Chicago was mostly bur oak savanna, so what outlived Chicago's building is too.

trees.name: The Bur Oak on the Midway

location.address: Midway Plaisance at Ellis Avenue, Hyde Park, Chicago, IL

trees.story: When the Midway Plaisance was cleared and regraded for the 1893 World's Fair, one tree was left standing, and this is it. By then it was already substantial enough that the ecologist Henry Cowles used it in his 1901 textbook as the example of its kind. Accounts of the fair place it behind the Sitting Bull's Cabin exhibit and the ostrich farm concession, neither of which lasted the year. Sources disagree on how it got here, and it is worth stating both. The University of Chicago Magazine quotes a campus environment official describing it as ostensibly planted as part of a Native American exhibit during the fair itself. The better supported account, from the Hyde Park historian Gary Ossewaarde, from Cowles in 1901 and from a local history record of a 2024 trunk measurement, has it standing long before 1893 and deliberately spared. That measurement reportedly ran past the largest bur oak on the Morton Arboretum's own growth reference chart, which would push it beyond the 250 or so years usually quoted. Bur oak is the tree of the prairie edge in this part of Illinois, corky barked enough to survive the fires that kept the grassland open. This one is the last of that landscape left on the Midway. It stands near Ellis Avenue, in front of the university hospital, on a pin that is close rather than surveyed.
trees.access: Free, public park path along the Midway Plaisance
trees.transport: Metra Electric District to 59th St/University of Chicago station, about 22 minutes from Millennium Station downtown, then a short walk to Ellis Ave and the Midway
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one big bur oak standing on the open Midway Plaisance at Ellis Avenue, left where it was when everything around it was regraded for the 1893 fair.

trees.name: The Bur Oak Grove of Wooded Island
trees.age_estimate: the grove's oldest survivors are roughly 200 to 300 years

location.address: Wooded Island, Jackson Park, south end near the Clarence Darrow Bridge and Osaka Garden (6200 S. Cornell Ave area), Chicago, IL

trees.story: One of these oaks blew down around 2016, and its rings were counted back to roughly 1730. It had been standing for nearly three centuries when it fell. The ones still up are of the same generation: DNAinfo reported 250 year old bur oaks across the island, with a red oak of about 150 among them. Wooded Island is the part of the 1893 World's Fair that was deliberately left alone. Frederick Law Olmsted kept buildings off it entirely while the Court of Honor went up in white plaster to the south, and fair era painters kept turning their backs on the architecture to paint these oaks instead. The island sits on an undisturbed sand ridge, which is why the soil under the trees was never scraped and rebuilt the way the rest of Jackson Park was. In 2016 the Army Corps of Engineers spent 8.1 million dollars restoring the habitat here and wrote the old bur oaks into the plan, along with roughly 120 bur oak saplings that had seeded themselves around their parents. An oak stand actually reproducing inside a city is a rare thing to stand in. The place to stand is the path just south of the Osaka Garden, looking into the south end of the island, where the grove reads as one thing rather than as scattered trees.

best_time.label: September and October, when the big fringed bur oak acorns come down

trees.access: Free, public park, Chicago Park District (Wooded Island / Osaka Garden)
trees.transport: Metra Electric District to 59th St/University of Chicago station, about 22 minutes from downtown, then roughly a 15 to 20 minute walk east across Jackson Park to Wooded Island; or CTA bus to the Museum of Science and Industry and cross the Clarence Darrow Bridge
trees.how_to_recognise: You are looking for a grove rather than one tree: bur oaks of around 250 years with their own saplings seeded around them. Stand on the path just south of the Osaka Garden, at the island's south end.

trees.name: The Bur Oak Savanna of Union Ridge Cemetery
trees.age_estimate: the oldest estimated at 325 to 375 years, based on trunk size

location.address: Union Ridge Cemetery, 6700 W Higgins Ave, Chicago, IL 60656

trees.story: The oldest oak in this grove has been estimated at 325 to 375 years, which would make it roughly two centuries older than the city around it. It was already a mature prairie tree when Chicago was a portage and a fort. The figure comes from Scott Carlini, quoted in a 2016 hunt for the city's oldest tree, and it is based on trunk diameter rather than a ring core, so treat it as directional. We found no second independent estimate, which is why this entry stays flagged. What is solid is the setting. Union Ridge took its first burial in 1841 and is described by the Norwood Park Historical Society as the oldest continuously operating cemetery in Chicago. The ground was open prairie before it was platted, and what stands here is a genuine relict bur oak savanna: widely spaced, heavy limbed trees with daylight between them, which is what oaks look like when they grow up in grassland rather than in forest. Bur oak's thick corky bark let it survive the fires that kept that prairie open, and the graves that arrived in 1841 put an end to both the fires and the plough. It is a working cemetery, so come during posted visiting hours and behave like a guest. The pin is the entrance; the old section and its oaks are inside the grounds.
trees.access: Free, cemetery grounds open to visitors during posted hours
trees.transport: Metra Union Pacific Northwest Line to Norwood Park station, about 22 minutes from Ogilvie Transportation Center downtown, then a short walk
trees.how_to_recognise: You are looking for a savanna rather than one tree, widely spaced bur oaks with heavy limbs and daylight between them, which is how oaks grow up in grassland. They stand in Union Ridge Cemetery.

trees.name: The Champion Boxelder of Edgebrook

location.address: Edgebrook Golf Course, 6100 N Central Ave, Chicago, IL 60646 (Forest Preserves of Cook County)

trees.story: Boxelder is the tree nobody wants. It seeds itself into alleys and back lots, drops limbs, hosts the boxelder bugs that get into houses in autumn, and is generally written off as a weed that never lives long enough to get big. This one is the biggest known in Illinois. The state's Big Tree Register, run by University of Illinois Extension, ranks it champion of its species: just over nine feet around the trunk, 55 feet tall, a crown spreading 35 feet, and 172.3 points on the register's scoring formula, ahead of the runner up down in Shawnee National Forest at the far southern end of the state. It was measured and listed in 2026 with a dated photograph, so it is standing now. One honesty note, and it is the reason this entry is flagged: the register is the only source we could find on it. The Sun-Times feature on the state's big trees, the Extension's own announcement and the Forest Preserves champion list all fail to mention it, most likely because the title is very new. No Illinois register carries an age field either, so nobody has dated this tree and we are not going to guess at it. Visiting is a golf question. It stands on Edgebrook Golf Course, a public course run by the Forest Preserves of Cook County, which normally means a green fee to walk the fairways, and whether it can be seen from the perimeter is unconfirmed.
trees.access: Public 18-hole golf course, Forest Preserves of Cook County; a green fee is generally needed to walk the course itself, and whether the tree is visible from a public perimeter trail was not confirmed
trees.transport: Metra Milwaukee District North Line to Edgebrook station, the last stop still inside Chicago city limits, roughly 30 minutes from Chicago Union Station, then about a 15 to 20 minute walk east on Devon/Central Ave to the golf course entrance
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the state-champion box elder, an unusually large specimen of a species normally dismissed as a weed tree, about 2.7m round and 55 feet tall. It stands on Edgebrook Golf Course.

trees.name: The Champion Red Pine of Indian Boundary

location.address: Indian Boundary Golf Course, 8600 W Forest Preserve Ave, Chicago, IL 60634 (Forest Preserves of Cook County)

trees.story: This is the state champion red pine of Illinois, and it holds the title partly for want of competition. The Illinois Big Tree Register lists exactly one red pine anywhere in the state, and this is the one, standing on the Indian Boundary golf course on Chicago's northwest side. Its 153.52 points come from a trunk 6.8 feet around, a height of 64 feet and a crown spreading 31.5 feet, measured and listed in 2026, which doubles as the freshest evidence that it is alive and thriving. Nobody has dated it. Red pine is a northern species, well outside its natural range down here, so this is a planted tree rather than a relic of anything, and the register carries no age field for any entry. Any figure attached to this tree is worked backwards from its trunk rather than measured, and should be read that way. What is documented is the size, and for Pinus resinosa the giveaway is the needles: paired, three to six inches long, snapping cleanly in half when you bend one. Access is the honest problem. Indian Boundary is a public 18 hole course run by the Forest Preserves of Cook County, so walking the fairways generally means paying a green fee, and whether the tree can be seen or reached from outside the course was not established. Ask at the clubhouse before planning the trip.
trees.access: Public 18-hole golf course, Forest Preserves of Cook County; a green fee is generally needed to walk the course itself, and whether the tree is visible from a public perimeter path was not confirmed
trees.transport: Metra Milwaukee District West Line to River Grove or Elmwood Park, roughly 20 minutes from Chicago Union Station; or CTA/Pace bus along Forest Preserve Dr/Cumberland Ave. Exact walk time from the nearest stop to the tree was not verified.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the only red pine listed on Illinois' Big Tree Register, paired needles that snap cleanly in half, a trunk about 2m round and 64 feet tall. It stands on Indian Boundary Golf Course.

trees.name: The Kenilworth Witness Oak

location.address: 427 N Kenilworth Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302 (village parkway, Hemingway District)
location.neighbourhood: Oak Park (day trip from Chicago, not within city limits)

trees.story: Local history holds that this bur oak was a witness tree, a landmark the Potawatomi used to find the route back to the Des Plaines River after a hunt. Oak Park's own paper, the Wednesday Journal, reported that reading in 2014 along with the claim that it is the oldest parkway tree in the village. Its age depends on which article you open. The 2014 survey puts it at about 230 years. A 2011 piece in the same paper, written when Openlands and the Morton Arboretum gathered its acorns for a historic oak propagation project, calls it three centuries old. That is a gap of seventy years, nobody has resolved it, and both figures stand here rather than one being quietly chosen. There is a harder caveat. No source has confirmed this tree alive since that 2014 article. In October 2025 another Oak Park heritage bur oak of the same generation, over on Forest Avenue, was removed after disease took it. That was a different tree at a different address, but the cohort is visibly failing, so go expecting an oak and not a guarantee. It stands on the parkway, the village-owned strip between sidewalk and street, in front of a private house on North Kenilworth Avenue in the Hemingway district. Public ground, so stay on the pavement. Oak Park is not Chicago but the suburb immediately west, 20 to 25 minutes from the Loop on the Green Line.
trees.access: Free, public parkway tree (the strip of village-owned land between sidewalk and street), viewable from the public right of way; it fronts a private residence so stay on the parkway/sidewalk
trees.transport: CTA Green Line to Oak Park Ave station, roughly 20 to 25 minutes from the Loop, then about a 10 minute walk north; alternatively Metra Union Pacific West Line to Oak Park station
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands, on the village parkway strip between sidewalk and street outside 427 N Kenilworth Avenue. Nobody has confirmed it alive since 2014, so go expecting an oak and not a guarantee.

trees.name: The Sugar Maple of Busse Forest South

location.address: Busse Forest South, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
This sugar maple stands 36.6 metres tall, 120 feet, and the Forest Preserves of Cook County rank it second among all the sugar maples on their land. Their champion tree register measured it on 25 August 2023: a trunk 2.47 metres round at chest height, and a crown spreading 22 metres one way and only 12 the other.

That shape is what makes it worth the walk. A trunk under two and a half metres round is slim for a tree of this height, and the narrow crown tells the same story: this maple went up rather than out. Compare the Comfort Maple in Pelham, Ontario, another sugar maple on our map, whose trunk is six metres round. The Busse tree carries well under half that girth, yet the county's champion hackberry at Thatcher Woods, the biggest of its kind on preserve land, is recorded at exactly the same 120 feet.

Busse Forest South holds two more ranked trees: the county's champion basswood, about two and a half kilometres to the west, and its third-ranked basswood a little further north. Three register trees in one preserve make an afternoon of it.

The register records size, rank and place, and nothing about age. Nobody has dated this maple. If you know how old it is, or what stood here before the preserve, tell us. Come in October, when sugar maples colour.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, 36.6 metres on a trunk only 2.47 metres round, with a narrow crown. It stands at the register's point in Busse Forest South, about 2.4 km east of the champion basswood.

best_time.label: October, when the sugar maple turns orange and red

trees.name: The Silver Maple of Thatcher Woods

location.address: Thatcher Woods, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
This silver maple's trunk is 4.27 metres round, and in October 2023 the Forest Preserves of Cook County measured it as the second-biggest silver maple on all their land. It stands 26.8 metres tall, with a crown about 18.6 metres across one way and 13 the other.

Four metres of girth is a lot of trunk for a silver maple. On our own map, the Silver Maple of Wołoska in Warsaw measures 3.39 metres round at 20 metres tall, and Bruges' Canada Tree, planted in 1947, measures 2.44. Only two silver maples we list with a recorded girth are thicker: one in Warsaw's Park Zaslawa Malickiego at 5.02 metres, and Montreal's McKenna Silver Maple at 5.81.

What makes Thatcher Woods unusual is the company. Within 80 metres of this maple the register lists two more ranked trees, both hackberries: the county's champion, and its second-ranked, which at 39 metres is the taller of the two. Three register trees inside one short loop make this the easiest stop of the lot.

The register gives size, rank and place, and nothing more: no planting date, no history, no age. Nobody has dated this maple. If you know how old it is, or have photographs of it from years back, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the thick trunk, 4.27 metres round, on a maple about 27 metres tall. It stands in Thatcher Woods roughly 30 metres from the taller second-ranked hackberry.

trees.name: The Champion Hackberry of Thatcher Woods

location.address: Thatcher Woods, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
This is the biggest hackberry the Forest Preserves of Cook County have on their land, ranked first in their champion tree register. Measured in November 2023, it stands 36.6 metres tall on a trunk 3.51 metres round, under a crown about 22 metres wide in both directions.

For scale, the only other hackberry of this species we have measured is the Leaning Hackberry of Parco Treves in Padua: 1.55 metres round and 9 metres tall. The Thatcher Woods champion has more than twice its girth and four times its height.

It is not even the tallest hackberry in these woods. About 66 metres away stands the county's second-ranked hackberry, slimmer at 3.35 metres round but taller at 39 metres. The register still ranks the thicker, wider tree first. A silver maple ranked second in the county stands between the two, so three register trees share one short stretch of woodland.

Another hackberry, at National Grove, matches this trunk exactly at 3.51 metres and ranks third, two and a half metres shorter.

The register says nothing about age, and nobody has dated this tree. If you know how old it is, or have watched it over the years, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the broad crown, about 22 metres across both ways, over a 3.51 metre trunk. It stands in Thatcher Woods some 66 metres from the taller, slimmer second-ranked hackberry.

trees.name: The Hackberry of National Grove

location.address: National Grove, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
Of the three hackberries at the top of the Forest Preserves of Cook County's champion register, this one has the widest crown: about 23.5 metres one way and 21.6 the other, measured in December 2023. The register places it third among all the hackberries on preserve land.

Its trunk is 3.51 metres round, exactly the girth of the county champion at Thatcher Woods, about seven kilometres to the north. What separates them is height. The champion stands 36.6 metres, this tree 34.1, and the second-ranked hackberry at Thatcher Woods reaches 39. Three trees of one species, within 16 centimetres of each other in girth and all past 34 metres tall: Cook County grows hackberries big.

The gap with the rest of our map is wider. The only other hackberry of this species we have measured, the Leaning Hackberry of Parco Treves in Padua, is 1.55 metres round and 9 metres tall. National Grove's tree is nearly four times as tall, and its crown spans more than two and a half times the Padua tree's whole height.

Unlike the Thatcher pair, it has no ranked neighbour on our map. It is a stop of its own.

The register records size, rank and site, and no age. Nobody has dated this hackberry. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 23.5 by 21.6 metres, the widest of the county's top three hackberries, over a 3.51 metre trunk. It stands at the register's point in National Grove.

trees.name: The White Oak of Red Gate Woods

location.address: Red Gate Woods, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
The champion white oak of the Forest Preserves of Cook County is not the thickest white oak they have measured. It wins on everything else. When the register's surveyors measured it in May 2024, they recorded a trunk 4.21 metres round, a height of 29.3 metres and a crown about 23 metres across in both directions, nearly a perfect circle.

The county's second-ranked white oak, at McClaughrey Springs Woods about five kilometres to the southeast, has the fatter trunk at 4.76 metres. It is also eight metres shorter and narrower in the crown, and the register puts Red Gate Woods first.

Our map holds some famous white oaks to measure it against. The Devil's Den Witness Tree at Gettysburg is 4.11 metres round, a whisker thinner than this one. The Ruxton Liberty Tree in Baltimore reaches 5.49 metres and the Travilah Oak outside Washington 5.82. Red Gate Woods' champion does not match those two for girth. What it has is balance: height, trunk and crown together, enough to make it the county's champion.

The register gives size, rank and site, and no age, and girth alone is a poor clock for an oak. Nobody has dated this one. If you know how old it is, or have a core count, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the round, even crown, about 23 metres across both ways, over a 4.21 metre trunk and 29.3 metres of height. It stands at the register's point in Red Gate Woods.

trees.name: The White Oak of McClaughrey Springs Woods

location.address: McClaughrey Springs Woods, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
This white oak is 4.76 metres round at chest height, more than half a metre thicker than the county's champion white oak, and it still ranks second. The Forest Preserves of Cook County measured it in June 2024.

What it lacks is height. The champion at Red Gate Woods, about five kilometres to the northwest, is thinner at 4.21 metres but stands 29.3 metres tall. This one stops at 21, with a crown about 21 metres one way and 17 the other. Short and heavy against tall and even: the register prefers the second, a visitor may well prefer the first.

For comparison, the Devil's Den Witness Tree at Gettysburg, another white oak on our map, is 4.11 metres round. The Ruxton Liberty Tree in Baltimore, at 5.49, and the Travilah Oak near Washington, at 5.82, are bigger still, but McClaughrey Springs' oak is in that company.

The surveyors left two notes. It stands at the edge of a trail, which makes it easy to reach. And it shows some branch dieback, which is worth knowing before you go and worth telling us about if you see it worsen.

The register gives no age, and nobody has dated this oak. If you know how old it is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 4.76 metres round, on a short oak of 21 metres with some dead branches. It stands at the edge of a trail in McClaughrey Springs Woods.

trees.name: The Sassafras of Thorn Creek Division

location.address: Thorn Creek Division, Forest Preserves of Cook County, Illinois

trees.access: Free, a Forest Preserves of Cook County site open to the public (register Public_Access: Yes).
trees.story:
This sassafras is only 12.2 metres tall, and its trunk is 3.26 metres round. That makes it the biggest sassafras the Forest Preserves of Cook County have on their land, ranked first in their champion register when it was measured in July 2024.

Those two numbers sit oddly together, which is the reason to go. Set it beside another tree on our Chicago page, the county's second-ranked sugar maple at Busse Forest South: the maple is three times as tall, at 36.6 metres, and its trunk is thinner, at 2.47. The sassafras put its growth into girth. The crown follows suit, about 13 metres one way and 9 the other, low and compact over a trunk that would look at home on a tree twice its height.

It stands far from the other champions on this page, at Thorn Creek Division in southern Cook County, so it is a trip of its own rather than a stop on a walk.

The only other sassafras on our map stands in Green-Wood Cemetery in Brooklyn, and we hold no measurement for it, so for now this is the one with numbers.

The register gives no age, and nobody has dated this tree. If you know how old it is, tell us. Come in October, when sassafras turns orange and red.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the thick trunk, 3.26 metres round, on a low tree only about 12 metres tall with a compact crown. It stands at the register's point in Thorn Creek Division.

best_time.label: October, when the mitten-shaped leaves turn orange and red
